title: これは俺らの問題だ  (This Is Our Problem)

segments.t: Walking home in the middle of the day after losing his job, Muranishi discovers his marriage has fallen apart too. After a bitter argument, Sachiko packs up to leave the house, taking Mayumi and little Daisuke with her. Listen to this painful turning point.
何でそんなところにいるのよ？
幸子、どういうことだ？
嫌だ！もう終わりよ。
みっともない！
みっともないのはあんたでしょ！
俺のどこがみっともないんだ！
パパ！ラジコンは？カウンタックは？
大輔、ごめんな。
これは俺らの問題だ。
母さんは口を出すな！
大輔、行くよ！
ほら、早く行って！
Even during a heated breakup, Japanese relies on compact everyday patterns. Let's look at how each line works.
何でそんなところにいるのよ？
'Why are you standing there?' "Sonna tokoro" means 'a place like that', followed by "ni iru", to be there, and sharp feminine "no yo" demanding an explanation.
幸子、どういうことだ？
'Sachiko, what is the meaning of this?' Whenever something shocking happens and you want an explanation, "dou iu koto da" literally asks 'what kind of thing does this say?'
嫌だ！
'No!' Strong "iya da" expresses visceral refusal or distress—'I hate this!' or 'no way!'—much stronger than a polite 'no thank you'.
みっともない！
'How shameful!' "Mittomonai" criticizes behaviour or appearances as undignified, embarrassing, or unseemly.
みっともないのはあんたでしょ！
'You are the one who is shameful!' Turning "mittomonai" into "mittomonai no wa" spotlights 'the shameful one', and "desho" snaps back 'is you, obviously!'
俺のどこがみっともないんだ！
'What part of me is shameful!' Literally "ore no doko ga" asks 'where of me?'—the natural Japanese way to challenge someone with 'just what is wrong with me?!'
パパ！ラジコンは？カウンタックは？
'Papa! What about my remote-control car? What about the Countach?' With a sad little voice, Daisuke uses "rajikon", remote-control toy, plus rising "wa" to ask 'what about my car?'
大輔、ごめんな。
'Daisuke, I am sorry.' Built around casual "gomen", sorry, "gomen na" is how a parent or close friend apologizes softly, gentler than formal "sumimasen".
母さんは口を出すな！
'Stay out of this, Mother!' "Kuchi o dasu" literally means 'stick your mouth out'—a vivid idiom for meddling or butting into someone else's business!
大輔、行くよ！
'Daisuke, we are leaving!' Simple dictionary-form "iku", to go, plus "yo" tells a child 'come on, we are going now'. Now let's listen to the whole confrontation at the house again.
何でそんなところにいるのよ？
幸子、どういうことだ？
嫌だ！もう終わりよ。
みっともない！
みっともないのはあんたでしょ！
俺のどこがみっともないんだ！
パパ！ラジコンは？カウンタックは？
大輔、ごめんな。
これは俺らの問題だ。
母さんは口を出すな！
大輔、行くよ！
ほら、早く行って！

Notice "dou iu koto" for 'what does this mean?', "gomen na" for a warm personal apology, and "kuchi o dasu"—sticking your mouth in—for meddling. Next, the empty house triggers a memory from Muranishi's childhood.
さようなら。
